# 08-fresco — sources

Back-test entry `08-fresco.yaml`: Fresco, the AI scribe for construction superintendents (YC Fall 2024).
Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim from the page named; "Author's choice" marks the
smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent.

Main sources:
- [HN] Launch HN: Fresco (YC F24), 2024-11-21 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42204939
- [LYC] Launch YC: Fresco, the scribe for construction, 2024-10-23 — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/M73-fresco-the-scribe-for-construction
- [YCP] YC company page — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/fresco (now "AI-powered takeoff and estimating for Division 8 construction")
- [KOE] A contractor's daily-log expectations on Procore's support site — https://support.procore.com/tc/Koester/Site_Map/Koester_Expectations_-_Daily_Logs
- [SWI] Swiftask, Procore daily reports page (vendor) — https://swiftask.ai/ai-integration/procore/intelligent-daily-reports
- [BLS] BLS Occupational Outlook, construction managers — https://www.bls.gov/ooh/management/construction-managers.htm
- [OPU] Launch HN: Opusense (field reports for site inspectors), 2025-05-20 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44042791

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Construction superintendents on commercial jobs.
   [HN] "Superintendents are the busiest and most expensive people on construction sites."
   [LYC] "That’s the reality for 210k+ construction superintendents (or supervisors, foremen, PMs, etc.) across the USA."
   → `roles[superintendent]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: "on commercial jobs" (the founders ask
   for introductions to commercial general contractors in [LYC]).

2. **What (the job).** Keep the record of the day's work, for liability and disputes.
   [HN] "30-200 photos per day to document site progress (mostly for liability reasons, or in case of a dispute with the
   owner over delays and deliverables)"; photos used to create "daily logs", "structured documents that account for the
   work done on site on any given day". [KOE] the log is "a critical piece of documentation in the arbitration of a
   dispute". → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At the end of the day, after the site walks, in the trailer.
   [HN] "At the end of the day, they'll spend a few hours uploading those photos into OneDrive, or project management
   software like Procore or ACC." [YCP] "We were curious what superintendents were doing for hours in their trailers at
   the end of the day." [LYC] "supes are spending up to 3 hours a day creating documents". → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: daily log`.
   Author's choice: the recall window {5, WORKING_DAYS} and Frequency 4 to 5 working days out of 5 (the posts say "per
   day"; a five-day site week is assumed). Prevalence `p_80_100` ("Nearly all") follows from the same "per day".

4. **Which people (the comparable group).** Superintendents at US general contractors whose jobs run on Procore or ACC.
   [LYC] "210k+ construction superintendents ... across the USA"; "Project management tools like Procore and ACC have
   dramatically increased documentation requirements". [YCP] "driving to Napa, South Bay, and around SF". → `context.segment`,
   `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The general contractor, per site.
   [HN] "we charge per site per month, which includes unlimited users on any given construction project".
   → `persona.decision_maker: {role: contractor}`, the BUYER role. Author's choice: the decider is the contractor's
   "operations lead" and the role to test is "The CFO" (a second role, "The project executive", listed); Purchase
   friction's three steps ("A trial on one live job" tested, a Procore check, a security review) and Commitment's step
   "start a paid pilot on one site" are the author's. Public material names no buyer title; [LYC] asks for
   introductions to general contractors by firm, not by role.

6. **Mechanism.** Narrated short videos turned into notes, texted to the crew, pushed to Procore/ACC.
   [HN] "Supers simply take short videos with voiceover, or upload photos, and Fresco does the rest, creating notes with
   transcription, photos, assignees, and due dates. Supers can easily text their crew action items, and receive texts
   back". "We also route this to whatever project management software they're using with a single click."
   [LYC] the narrated example "The beam in the southwest corner of room 134 is corroded and needs replacement by Alex.";
   "Supes who use Fresco complete their notes, on average, 90% faster."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility and Adoption friction items. Relative advantage's two
   benefits are from [HN] ("during their site walks, not after") and [LYC] ("90% faster"); their wording is the author's.

7. **Price.** About $1k per site per month, less with multi-site or multi-month terms.
   [HN] "The typical price is $1k/month, but we offer discounts for multi-month or multi-site commitments."
   → `commercial.price` {800, 1000, month}. Author's choice: the low end of $800 stands for the stated discounts.
   Existing sacrifice: 30 to 60 hours a month per site at an hourly rate of 55 — from [LYC] "up to 3 hours a day" and
   [HN] "a few hours uploading", taken as 1.5 to 3 hours on about twenty working days (author's arithmetic). The rate is
   [BLS] "$55.28 per hour" (median, construction managers, May 2025), the author's stand-in: no superintendent wage is
   in the public material. Ability to pay is derived by code (24% to 61%).

8. **Occasions.** The narrated beam; a school refit report; the uploads and logs at the end of the day.
   [LYC] on a school refit walkthrough: "Normally, creating the final report takes 2+ hours."
   [HN] "few supers have time to do this thoroughly, so these photos aren't very searchable." No named customer quote
   exists in public; the occasions below are scripted from these and from practitioner comments.

## Open
- The verdict was scripted to be plausible and not obviously "build": the problem holds on how often but people
  disagree on whether the log is one of their two worst difficulties; the solution splits on the benefit and on
  talking over videos on site; the price fails (two of eight at the founder's band or above) while the cost it would
  replace is above the price. This is the author's reading of the thread's sceptics, not a measured result.
- No public account names a buyer title at a general contractor; the decider, the tested role "The CFO", the purchase
  steps and the Commitment step are the author's.
- hourly_rate 55 is a proxy (construction managers, not superintendents).
- Existing sacrifice picks use `period: quarter` (the corpus's convention), although the registry's recall period for a
  monthly cost reads "last month"; the values are the monthly figures times three.
- The window {5, WORKING_DAYS} is the author's; the public posts say "per day".

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Each pair belongs together, since Renee and Omar both want proof before paying, and Faith and Trevor both say today's log cost is too small to pay much from, while the three left alone make separate points about per-site pricing, legal liability and paying twice, and the group names are plain.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line; all seven are about price, so nothing needed keeping out.

founder.order_why: The flow runs sensibly from context to problem, idea, buyer and sending, but the screens on how contractors answer and who gets a link are labelled 'Interviews · Sent', as if the study had already gone out before I'd said who receives it.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 20-21 (first real step, which for me is a paid pilot on one site) and screen 22 (Offer a pilot?) cover much the same ground; screens 3 and 4 also carry the same heading, but I can't tell from that whether they ask the same thing.
founder.missing: No screen visibly asks what the price is charged per; mine is per site per month with unlimited users, with discounts for multi-site or multi-month terms, and that changes how a contractor weighs it.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: It moves sensibly from whether I qualify, to the idea, to our current hours on the log, then to value, who signs off, how long a trial takes, and finally whether I'd start a paid pilot.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: What we pay today for anything covering the daily log, and how Fresco would be charged across sites, such as whether users are unlimited and whether there is a contract term.

screens.why1: Right after settling who has to agree, it makes sense to ask what could slow or stop a contractor buying Fresco.
screens.why2: The question is short, and approvals, reviews, procurement and switching are all words I use when selling to general contractors.
screens.why3: I know this from selling to GCs: the trial on a live job, the Procore check and the security review are the hurdles I expect.
screens.why4: The only chip is the escape, and leaving this out of the study is a fair choice for a founder who doesn't want to test it.
screens.why5: I typed three hurdles, but the belief keeps only the trial, drops the Procore check and security review, and adds a 2-week limit I never typed on this screen.
screens.instead: What could slow down or stop a purchase, and which one step would you test first and how long should it take? e.g. a trial on one live job, about 2 weeks.

screens.why1: Right after I named what could slow a purchase, it's obvious why Keel plays those steps back for me to check before the study tests them.
screens.why2: The rows are in my own words, but the belief's tail, "or not need it", needs a second read, and it isn't obvious whether the rows or the belief are the thing I'm being asked to check.
screens.why3: As the founder selling to general contractors, I know what stands between a yes and a signed deal on a job: a trial, the Procore fit and a security review.
screens.why4: The three rows are distinct and complete as the main hurdles, each is short enough for the limit, and I can reword, remove or add to them.
screens.why5: The three steps are kept as I gave them, but my material gives no two-week figure for the trial, so that number reads as Keel's rather than mine.
screens.instead: What has to happen before a contractor signs up? A trial on one live job / A check that it works with Procore / A security review. Belief to check: most operations leads could finish a trial on one live job within about 2 weeks, or would skip the trial.

screens.why1: Right after I named what could slow a purchase, it makes sense to pick the one step to test and say how long I expect it to take.
screens.why2: It is nearly all plain, but "how long would this step take before it went through" reads oddly for a trial, and I need a second read to tell whether it means the trial's run or the time to get it approved and finished.
screens.why3: I sell to general contractors per site, so I can pick the step and estimate from my own sales conversations how long a trial on one job takes.
screens.why4: The three steps are the ones I gave and are distinct, a Procore check and a security review are real hurdles at a GC, and days, weeks or months cover the likely answers.
screens.why5: The trial on one live job and my 2 weeks are kept, and "or not need it" fairly allows for a buyer who would skip the trial.
screens.instead: Keep the screen, but ask: "If they bought it, how long would this step take from start to finish?"

screens.why1: After who decides, cost, price, who must agree and what could stall the purchase, asking what first real step I want from the buyer is the obvious last commercial question.
screens.why2: The question and hint are plain, and 'costs them time, data, money or a signature' tells me at once what counts as a real step.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I want from a contractor because we sell per site, so a paid pilot on one job is the step I would actually ask for.
screens.why4: The only chip, 'Leave this out of the study', is a fitting escape for a founder who does not want to test a commitment step, and the free-text box covers the answer.
screens.why5: My 'start a paid pilot on one site' is kept word for word in the belief, and 'the contractor operations lead' is the decider I named earlier.

screens.why1: Right after I set the first real step and on the way to sending, it makes sense to decide whether strangers get asked to try it for real.
screens.why2: The question and the hint are short and plain, and they tell me exactly what people see and where I see the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want to offer a pilot is my own call, and I already run paid site pilots with contractors.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers the choice, the two options are distinct, and no escape is needed for a founder's own decision.
screens.why5: I typed 'Start a paid pilot on one site', but the screen's line says only 'Would you try this for real? Leave your email', so it loses the paid and one-site parts of my step.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes get a line at the end: "Would you start a paid pilot on one site? Leave your email." You see who said yes on the Pilot tab. Options: Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Right before sending, choosing who fronts the interview is an obvious last setup step, and it comes after the study itself is settled.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint packs in video, typing, credits and the text link, and 'Keel records the voice you pick once' sits oddly on a screen where I am picking a video face.
screens.why3: I can decide this: I know my supers and can hear both samples, and the 400 credits are my own spend.
screens.why4: Two named interviewers with 5-second samples are distinct and enough, but nothing tells me how they differ before I tap, and there is no chip for sending the written form only.
screens.why5: It keeps my 'construction superintendents' and adds nothing about Fresco, and the preselected Daphne matches the choice I made to take Keel's pick.
screens.instead: Who should ask construction superintendents your questions on video? Daphne is picked for you; tap Saskia to hear her and switch. Either costs 400 credits, once for this project. People can read and tap or type instead of talking. Options: Daphne ▶ 5 s; Saskia ▶ 5 s.

screens.why1: Right after choosing how superintendents get asked, it's obvious that the buyer side needs its own answer format before the study goes out.
screens.why2: The question and choices are plain, but "Still recording · ready in a few minutes" takes a second read because it doesn't say what is recording or what I'd be waiting for.
screens.why3: I know how contractor operations leads work, reading and tapping between emails and calls, so I can decide this from what I know.
screens.why4: The three choices are distinct and cover the real ways to answer, and the readiness notes help me weigh them, with no escape chip needed for a founder's setup choice.
screens.why5: I set the person answering as the contractor's operations lead, and "contractors" shortens that to the firm, though the meaning still holds.
screens.instead: How should contractor operations leads answer? AI interviewer · Daphne (her video is still being made, ready in a few minutes) / Read and tap (ready now) / Let them choose (ready when Daphne's video is).

screens.why1: I've just chosen how contractors will answer, so the obvious next step before sending is deciding who gets the link.
screens.why2: The question and all three options are plain on first reading, and the mention of Keel's Contacts page is clear because it is named as a place to search.
screens.why3: I know whether I'm sending to contractors I know by name, a Keel list or an open group, and I can answer from the relationships I actually have.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover how I'd reach people, and my usual route of introductions to contractors still fits under a named person's own link once I have the name.
screens.why5: My pick of people I know by name, each with their own link, is kept as I meant it, and nothing about Fresco or the buyer is changed.
screens.instead: Which contractors get a link? (same three options)

screens.why_b1: "Not holding up" sits at the top with the number that decides it right beside it: Price, 1 of 8 at $800 or more per site a month.
screens.why_b2: Each card gives its count and bar plainly (1 of 8, bar 6 of 8), but I need a second look to see why Existing sacrifice counts 7 of the 8 and how "not holding" differs from "did not hold" in the tally.
screens.why_b3: The names and the Buyer and payer, Purchase friction and Commitment lines are the ones I checked, but Existing sacrifice says operations leads spend the 30 to 60 hours, when my superintendents write the log and the firm pays for that time.
screens.why_b4: "They value it below your price" tells me where the idea breaks, but the page doesn't say what that means for my $800 to $1,000 per site or what to do next, such as rethinking the price or the pilot.
screens.why_b5: Counts and bars stay visible and at-the-bar results are marked, but "Holding up" on Existing sacrifice softly overstates it: exactly at the bar on 7 people, with a line that credits the hours to the operations leads.
screens.instead: Not holding up: only 1 of 8 operations leads would pay $800 or more a site a month, though 5 of 7 say the log already costs 30 hours or more a month on their sites; so test a lower price or a clearer tie to those hours before asking for a paid pilot, which only 3 of 8 would start now.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside 5 of 7 at 30 hours or more against a bar of 5 of 7, so I can see both the answer and that it only just clears.
screens.why_b2: The strip is labelled hours of the daily log per site a month, the cells show 5 for and 2 against out of 7, and the marker sits at 5 with the bar spelled out as at least 2 in 3.
screens.why_b3: The 30 to 60 hours per site a month is my number and the dimension is recognisable, but the line says the contractor operations leads spend the hours, when it's my superintendents who do the log and the leads only answer for the firm.
screens.why_b4: The So line says the cost is real at or above my low and that the open question is whether they would pay to remove it, which points me straight at Price.
screens.why_b5: The n, the exclusions and "a lean, not a call" are all visible, but "The cost is there" is flat for a result sitting exactly at the bar, where one person moving would flip it, and Trevor's unexplained 10.9 hours looks more exact than a recalled figure can be.
screens.instead: Superintendents' time on the daily log costs contractors 30 hours or more per site a month at 5 of 7 firms, exactly at your bar, so one answer would flip it: the cost looks real but this is a lean, and whether they would pay to remove it is the Price card.

screens.why_b1: "Not holding up" sits directly beside the deciding number, 1 of 8 at $800 or more against a bar of 6 of 8, so I know the answer and that it missed by a wide margin.
screens.why_b2: The bands show what each of the 8 contractor operations leads said it was worth, the for and against labels and strip make the 1 versus 7 split plain, and the bar at 6 of 8 and my price's band are marked.
screens.why_b3: The card is named Price and says $800 to $1,000 per site a month from contractor operations leads, which is my price, my unit and my buyer.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the result and sends me to the Insights tab, without saying what it means for $1k per site, even though the quotes on this screen point to the per-site fee, unproven hours and trust in the record.
screens.why_b5: All 8 answers stay visible, the small group is called a lean rather than a call, and "Fewer than 2 in 3" understates rather than overstates a 1 of 8 result.
screens.instead: Only 1 of 8 would value it at $800 or more and 5 put it under $500, so with this small group $1k per site looks too high: before changing the number, test per-super pricing and show buyers the logged hours, because several objected to the per-site fee or saw no cost to pay it from.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits directly above the number that decides it, 1 of 8 named my price with 5 needed, so I know there is no answer yet and why.
screens.why_b2: I can see at a glance that it counts where the money would come from and that one person answered, but I have to look twice at "your bar · 1 of 1 (at least 2 in 3)" because it reads as a bar of one person, while the strip's five cells and the "5 needed" say something else.
screens.why_b3: The price band and "contractor operations leads" are my own words and I recognise the idea, but Ability to pay is not among the beliefs I checked on the way in, so this line is Keel's wording rather than mine.
screens.why_b4: It tells me concretely that Price decides this stage, that only 1 of 8 would pay $800, and that this card means nothing until at least 5 name my price, so the price is the thing I have to deal with.
screens.why_b5: It makes no claim from Gordon's single answer: the 1 stays visible, the six who named less and Sandra are accounted for by name, and both the verdict and the "a small group: a lean, not a call" line say it is too few.
screens.instead: Bar: at least 2 in 3 of the 5 people needed; so far 1 person has answered, so there is nothing to read until the price question is settled.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside 6 of 8 and the bar of 6 of 8, so I can see the belief held and that it held exactly at the bar.
screens.why_b2: The four answers with their counts, the 8 people and the marker at 6 are plain at first look, and each row says for or against.
screens.why_b3: The title and the line that the operations lead decides and the CFO has to agree are the ones I checked, and the question uses my CFO and my $800 a site.
screens.why_b4: "Plan for the CFO in most deals" points me the right way, but it stops short of saying how, such as building the case for the CFO before a pilot, and says nothing about what the 2 who answered against mean for my sales path.
screens.why_b5: It says "a lean, not a call" and keeps n visible, but "Holding up" gets there by counting 2 who could sign alone toward a belief that the CFO has to agree, when only 4 of 8 said exactly that, and "most deals" stretches those 4 to all deals.
screens.instead: Holding up at the bar, but only just: 4 of 8 need the CFO, 2 could sign alone and 2 said others decide, so with 8 people bring a CFO case to each deal and ask early who else signs.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits directly above the deciding number, 3 of 8 expecting longer than 2 weeks against a bar of no more than 2 of 8.
screens.why_b2: The eight people and the duration bands are plain, but the bar needs a second look because the verdict says no more than 2 of 8 against while the chart and strip say 6 of 8 for.
screens.why_b3: Purchase friction and the belief line are exactly what I checked on the way in, with the trial on one live job and my 2 weeks intact.
screens.why_b4: It tells me concretely to plan for a trial cycle of 2 weeks to 1 month and points me to the Insights tab for what would take the time.
screens.why_b5: n is visible and the small group is called a lean, but "most often 2 weeks to 1 month" hides a 3-3 tie with 1 to under 2 weeks, and that band's low edge is exactly my 2 weeks, so "longer than 2 weeks" is slightly overstated.
screens.instead: Did not hold, by one person: 3 of 8 said 2 weeks to 1 month, 3 said 1 to under 2 weeks and 2 said it wouldn't be needed, so plan for up to a month on the slower deals, though with 8 people this is a lean.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside the deciding number: 3 of 8 said yes against a bar of 6 of 8, 3 short.
screens.why_b2: The chart plainly counts the eight operations leads' answers as 3 yes, 3 probably not and 2 no, and the strip's marker shows the bar at 6 of 8.
screens.why_b3: Commitment and the paid pilot on one site are the name and belief I checked, and the bar is the one Keel set, restated as no more than 1 in 3 saying probably not or no.
screens.why_b4: It tells me 5 of 8 would not start the pilot and points me to the Insights tab for what they would start with, but it does not say what this means for the idea or my pilot offer.
screens.why_b5: All eight answers stay visible by name, the screen says a small group is a lean and not a call, and it claims nothing beyond these people.
screens.instead: 5 of 8 ops leads wouldn't start a paid pilot on one site today (a lean from 8 people), so don't count on the paid pilot as your way in yet; see on the Insights tab what they'd start with instead and test that offer with the 3 who said yes and the 3 who said probably not.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its verdict with the deciding number beside it, such as Price not holding up at 1 of 8 against a bar of 6 and Commitment did not hold at 3 of 8 against a bar of 6, 3 short.
screens.why_b3: Price, Purchase friction and Commitment are the names I saw, and the belief lines are the ones I checked, including the paid pilot on one site and the trial on one live job within about 2 weeks.
screens.why_b4: The screen never says what these failures mean for Fresco or what to do next; I have to work out for myself that per-site pricing, a free first job and proof of hours are the things to change, and the two empty boxes offer no next step either.
screens.why_b5: The counts stay visible and every quote is named with its pick, nothing claims more than these 8 people, and the empty Purchase friction and Commitment boxes say plainly that 0 were asked there, who never saw the question and how many were asked on Price.
screens.why_b6: The quotes give me things I did not type: the per-site fee adds up across jobs and per-super pricing would go higher, it is a second fee on top of project software, a wrong note in a dispute lands on the contractor, and buyers want a free month or the hours shown first.

screens.why1: As the first question it makes sense to me as a check on whether my company's software setup fits the study, and I haven't been asked it before.
screens.why2: Procore and ACC are the platforms people in my job talk about every day, and "jobs that run on" is how we say it, so I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I choose and pay for the software our job sites use, so I know exactly which platforms our jobs run on.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it completely because using either platform counts as yes and using neither counts as no, and a screener like this needs no escape.
screens.why5: It names only the platforms I already know, and nothing about anyone's product, plan or labels for people reaches me.
screens.why6: Said aloud it is one short question, ACC says cleanly as three letters I use all the time, and I can answer yes or no after hearing it once.

screens.why1: After being asked whether we run jobs on Procore or ACC, showing me the idea before the buying questions makes obvious sense, and the kicker tells me that's where this is going.
screens.why2: Site walk, superintendents, assignees, Procore and ACC are all my language, but "AI scribe" is not a term I'd use and "notes from your site walk" barely tells me what the thing is on first read.
screens.why3: I know how my supers walk jobs, log the day and work in Procore or ACC, so I can picture this on my sites.
screens.why4: This is a card to read, with no options, rows, chips or value box.
screens.why5: An idea card is meant to show me the product, so nothing leaks, but the first line never says what Fresco is, and the belief line just repeats the how instead of pointing back to it, which reads like a founder's pitch.
screens.why6: It can be said and has no parenthesis or slash, but seven sentences is long for one hearing, "notes" repeats awkwardly at the end, and the belief line makes me hear the same list a second time.
screens.instead: Imagine Fresco, an app that turns site walk videos into notes. Your superintendents take short videos and talk over them, and it writes notes with photos, who's on it and due dates, texts the crew their items, and sends the notes to Procore or ACC in one click. The people building it believe this would save your supers from writing it all up afterward.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, I can see why they'd ask what the daily log costs us now, before getting into whether I'd buy anything.
screens.why2: Daily log, site and hours are everyday words for me, and I can tell it wants the month's total for one site, though I'd have to convert from the minutes per day I think in.
screens.why3: I pay for the tools but my supers write the logs, so I'd be estimating from what I know about how long they take and multiplying across about 20 workdays.
screens.why4: An hours box handles any real answer, and None and I can't recall are distinct and fit, since a site that logged nothing or a lead who doesn't know both have a way out.
screens.why5: It asks about our own daily log in our own words, with no product name or founder language coming through.
screens.why6: The question says well once, but the instruction 'A number of hours per site last month, or a low and a high; none is 0' is clipped, repeats the unit and is a mouthful to hear.
screens.instead: Last month, about how many hours did your team spend on the daily log at a typical site? A number of hours, or a low and a high. Or say you can't recall.

screens.why1: I've just seen the idea and said how much time the daily log takes, so asking what it's worth to me is the obvious next thing, and I'm the one who pays.
screens.why2: A monthly price per site is how I already think about job-site software, so I can answer this on first reading.
screens.why3: I pay for tools like this per job and know what our sites can carry, so I can put a figure on it from my own budget, though I'd be judging it from a one-line idea.
screens.why4: The bands don't overlap, they run from cheap to more than I'd ever pay, there's a clear way to say I wouldn't pay, and 'I can't say' fits as the escape.
screens.why5: The only product talk is the 'Imagine Fresco' card shown on purpose, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms for people reaches me.
screens.why6: It's one short question and the two-step amounts are easy to hold, but 'Or say you can't say' trips when heard because it sounds like I'm being told I can't say something.
screens.instead: Same question and options; said aloud, end with: Or say 'I can't say'.

screens.why1: It comes straight after I gave a price and follows up on that exact answer, so it is obvious why it is asked.
screens.why2: Short, plain words, and I can answer it on first reading or first hearing.
screens.why3: I pay for job-site software, so I know what would make a tool worth more per site, such as how much super time it saves and how well it fits Procore or ACC.
screens.why4: The screen is a box to type in, with no options, rows or chips.
screens.why5: It only repeats the name from the idea card and the price I gave, and nothing new about the product or how the founder thinks about people reaches me.
screens.why6: Two short sentences with one question, and the amount says well as five hundred to under eight hundred dollars, though the bundle records no spoken form for it.

screens.why1: I just put a price on it, so whether I could approve that money myself is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: Sign off, per site and CFO are how I talk about spend at a general contractor, and I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: I choose and pay for our site software, so I know exactly what I can approve alone and when finance has to agree.
screens.why4: The four options cover the real answers, though the CFO can also be one of the several people or the someone else, and the escape I can't recall one makes no sense because I'm not recalling anything.
screens.why5: Nothing about the founder's product or plan reaches me, and the $800 is simply the top of the band I just gave.
screens.why6: The stem and four options say well enough, but an either-or question answered with yes or no takes a moment by ear, and Or say you can't recall one sounds wrong when nothing has been asked to recall.
screens.instead: Could you sign off on about $800 per site a month yourself? Yes, on my own; no, the CFO would decide; no, several of us would have to agree; or no, someone else decides. Or say I can't say.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I could sign off on the money, it makes sense to ask what stands between saying yes and actually having this running on a job.
screens.why2: I know what a trial on a live job is, but a trial doesn't "go through" the way a purchase does, and "if you bought" before "a trial" has the order backwards, so I'd read it twice to work out whether you mean the length of the trial or the wait to get one started.
screens.why3: I've run new software on a live job before and I know about how long we test it before committing, so I can answer this from experience.
screens.why4: The range covers everything and "It wouldn't be needed" and "I can't tell" both fit, but exactly 1 month falls in both "2 weeks to 1 month" and "1 to 3 months".
screens.why5: A trial on one live job is how my trade would test a tool, and nothing here reaches me as the founder's plan or terms beyond the Fresco name I was already shown.
screens.why6: Heard aloud, it is one short question with four short options and one escape, then an easy two-way follow-up, so I can hold it and answer the first time.
screens.instead: If you bought Fresco, how long would you want to trial it on one live job before you'd roll it out? Under 1 week; 1 to under 2 weeks; 2 weeks to under 1 month; 1 to 3 months; Over 3 months; We wouldn't need a trial; I can't tell

screens.why1: It's the last question after price, sign-off and trial time, so it's obvious why you'd ask if I'd actually start a pilot.
screens.why2: A paid pilot on one site is how I'd normally try software on a job, so I can answer this on first read.
screens.why3: I choose and pay for our site software, so whether I'd start a paid pilot is my own call.
screens.why4: There's a plain yes but no "probably yes", so if I'd lean yes only once I'd seen the price and the details, I have to overstate it, and "Probably not" sits close to "No".
screens.why5: The card is shown on purpose and in plain words, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms for people reaches me.
screens.why6: It's one short question with three options I can hold after one hearing, and no escape is needed because "no" is the floor.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you start a paid pilot on one site, or not? Yes, I'd start one / Probably, once I'd seen the terms / Probably not / No
